title: Box Model and Layout Basics
summary: Every element on a page is a box made of content, padding, border, and margin. Learn how box-sizing changes what "width" means, why margins collapse, and how block/inline/inline-block decide layout before you ever touch flex or grid.

slides.markdown:
Before flexbox, before grid, every single HTML element renders as a **box**. That box has four layers stacked outward from the inside: content, padding, border, margin. Almost every CSS layout bug — "why is there a gap here," "why did my width overflow the container" — traces back to misreading one of these four layers.

This topic is the foundation the rest of the group builds on: positioning, flexbox, and grid all still obey the box model underneath. Get this wrong and every layout technique built on top of it produces surprises.

The two things that trip up almost everyone: `box-sizing` silently changes what "width" means, and vertical margins between siblings don't simply add — they **collapse**.

slides.subTitle: Content, padding, border, margin
slides.markdown:
Every box is four nested rectangles, from the inside out:

- **Content** — where text and child elements actually sit. This is what `width`/`height` set (by default).
- **Padding** — space inside the border, same background as the content. Padding is part of the element visually — click a padded area of a button and you hit the button.
- **Border** — a visible or invisible line wrapping the padding. Has its own `width`, `style`, `color`.
- **Margin** — transparent space *outside* the border, separating this box from its neighbors. Margin is never part of the element's own background or clickable area.

The distinction that matters most in practice: padding and border are **inside** the element (they're part of it, they show its background color), while margin is **outside** it (transparent, pushes other elements away, never paints).

slides.subTitle: What "width" actually measures
slides.markdown:
`box-sizing` decides which layers your `width`/`height` values describe.

- **`content-box`** (the CSS default): `width` sets *only the content box*. Padding and border are added on top. Set `width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 2px solid` and the box renders **244px** wide (200 + 20 + 20 + 2 + 2).
- **`border-box`**: `width` sets the *outer* edge, up to but not including margin. The same declaration renders exactly **200px** — padding and border eat into the content area instead of adding to it.

`content-box` is why a `width: 100%` element with any padding overflows its parent — the padding adds extra pixels the parent never accounted for. That single behavior is responsible for more accidental horizontal scrollbars than any other CSS default.

slides.subTitle: Why almost every team does this
How display decides participation in flow
slides.markdown:
`display` controls how a box interacts with the boxes around it, independent of the box model itself:

| Value | Width/height respected? | Starts new line? | Typical elements |
|---|---|---|---|
| **block** | Yes — full box model applies | Yes, stacks vertically | `div`, `p`, `section`, `h1` |
| **inline** | No — `width`/`height` are ignored | No, flows with text | `span`, `a`, `strong`, `em` |
| **inline-block** | Yes — full box model applies | No, flows with text | `img`, `button`, `input` |

Inline elements only respect **horizontal** padding/margin visually — vertical padding is applied but doesn't push surrounding line boxes apart, which is why padding a `<span>` vertically looks like it "overlaps" the line above and below it. `inline-block` exists specifically to get sizeable boxes (so you can set width/height and vertical margin) while keeping inline flow (so it sits next to text instead of forcing a line break).

slides.subTitle: The layout you get before flex/grid/position
slides.markdown:
With no `position`, `display: flex`, or `display: grid` applied, elements lay out in **normal flow**: block-level boxes stack top-to-bottom filling the full available width, and inline-level boxes flow left-to-right (in LTR languages) wrapping onto new lines as needed, like words in a paragraph.

Normal flow is the baseline every other layout mode is an *escape hatch* from. `position: absolute` removes an element from flow entirely — the elements around it act as if it isn't there. `float` (largely legacy now) pulls an element to one side and lets inline content wrap around it, while itself leaving normal flow. Flexbox and grid replace normal flow's rules for a container's *direct children* but the container itself, and anything outside it, still obeys normal flow.

Understanding normal flow first is what makes every other layout mode legible — each one is defined by what it changes relative to this default.

slides.subTitle: Why 20px + 20px isn't always 40px
slides.markdown:
Adjacent **vertical** margins between block-level elements in normal flow don't add — they **collapse** to the larger of the two. Stack two paragraphs, one with `margin-bottom: 20px` and the next with `margin-top: 30px`, and the gap between them is **30px**, not 50px.

This happens in three situations: between sibling elements, between a parent and its first/last child (if nothing separates them — no border, padding, or content), and between an empty element's own top and bottom margin.

Margin collapsing **only applies to vertical margins in normal flow** — horizontal margins never collapse, and margins inside a flex or grid container don't collapse either, which is one of the quieter reasons teams migrate spacing-heavy layouts to flexbox: `gap` gives predictable, non-collapsing spacing where margin was unreliable.

slides.sectionTitle: Stopping collapse when you need to
slides.markdown:
A parent/child margin collapse can leak margin *outside* a container that looks like it should contain it — a common surprise when a heading's `margin-top` appears to push the parent `div` down instead of adding space inside it.

Any of these break the parent-child collapse:

```css
.container {
  padding-top: 1px;      /* any padding separates the margins */
  border-top: 1px solid transparent; /* any border works too */
  overflow: hidden;       /* establishes a new block formatting context */
}
```

`overflow: hidden` (or `auto`) is the one developers reach for most, because it fixes collapsing *and* the classic "parent collapses to zero height around floated children" problem in one line — both are really the same root cause: the parent isn't establishing its own formatting context. Flexbox and grid containers never have this problem, since flex/grid items don't participate in margin collapsing at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Debugging "why isn't my width doing what I expect"
slides.subTitle: The interview-favorite bug
slides.markdown:
This is one of the most commonly asked live-debugging prompts in frontend interviews, precisely because it tests whether you actually understand the box model instead of having memorized it.

A reliable checklist, roughly in the order to check:

1. **Check `box-sizing`.** If it's `content-box` (the default, if no reset is applied), padding and border are adding to your set width — this explains the vast majority of "my box is wider than I set it" bugs.
2. **Check for inherited percentage widths against an unexpected parent.** A percentage width resolves against the *containing block*, which isn't always the visual parent (e.g. under `position: absolute`, it resolves against the nearest positioned ancestor).
3. **Check `display`.** An inline element silently ignoring your `width`/`height` reads exactly like a box-model bug but isn't one.
4. **Open DevTools' computed box model panel.** It shows the actual resolved content/padding/border/margin numbers, which settles layer 1–3 in seconds rather than guessing from source.

Saying this checklist out loud, in this order, is usually enough to pass the exercise — interviewers are grading the diagnostic process as much as the fix.

Everything past this point in the group assumes the box model as ground truth. `position` (next topic) changes how a box's final location is calculated, but the box itself still has content/padding/border/margin. Flexbox and grid change how a *container* distributes space among children, but each child is still a box with the same four layers — `flex-basis` and grid track sizing both interact directly with `box-sizing`.

The two habits worth keeping from this topic: default to `border-box` everywhere, and reach for DevTools' computed box model panel the moment a width or spacing value looks wrong, rather than guessing from the stylesheet.
